Daily Brief

Tensions between Washington and Kyiv dominated headlines as President Zelensky arrived in Brussels to rally European support after announcing Ukraine would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying President Trump's demands [BBC, RFI, Financial Times]. Trump responded sharply, calling Zelensky 'more difficult to deal with than Putin' and labeling the renewed attacks 'a disgrace' [BBC]. EU leaders closed ranks around Ukraine, with Commission President von der Leyen pledging to maintain sanctions and increase pressure on Moscow [Financial Times, BBC]. Meanwhile, ship attacks near the Strait of Hormuz reached record highs as the US-Israeli conflict with Iran intensifies, with 12 vessels reporting strikes in a single week [BBC]. A tragic school shooting in Bend, Oregon claimed the lives of three children and a teacher before an armed bystander killed the 16-year-old attacker [BBC, Le Monde, France 24]. In diplomatic developments, China's foreign minister urged Israel to halt West Bank settlement expansion, calling the Palestinian question 'the greatest historical injustice of this century' [BBC]. Guinea-Bissau denied approving a controversial hepatitis B vaccine trial promoted by RFK Jr., contradicting earlier reports [The Guardian].

Three Children and Teacher Killed in Oregon Elementary School Shooting

  • A 16-year-old shooter forced entry into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon by firing at locked doors on Thursday afternoon
  • Three children aged 5, 8, and 11, along with one teacher, were killed; a 7-year-old and another teacher remain in critical condition
  • An armed community member pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead; police arrived three minutes later

Ship Attacks Near Strait of Hormuz Hit Record High as Iran Conflict Escalates

  • Twelve vessels reported attacks between October 5-11, the highest weekly total since the US-Israeli war with Iran began, with six ships struck in a single day

04 Policy

Guinea-Bissau Denies Approving RFK Jr.-Backed Vaccine Trial in Newborns

  • Guinea-Bissau's health minister stated the government never authorized the controversial hepatitis B vaccine trial, contradicting earlier reports of approval
  • The study, championed by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., would withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some newborns to track 'nonspecific' health outcomes
  • A Danish research ethics committee had voted to proceed based on information that Guinea-Bissau had approved the trial
  • Critics have called the trial ethically problematic, with one physician stating Kennedy is 'taking advantage of a developing country'
